name: Dennis Allen

views.text: Defense should attack and take the fight to the offense instead of waiting to react.
Game planning is cooking with what is in the pantry: find what each player does well and ask him only for that.
Takeaways are earned through effort and pressure, not handed over by the offense.
When the fundamentals slip, the coordinator looks at himself first; a big install is no excuse.
Let players be themselves, as long as the defense stays physical and hard-nosed.
A coordinator who was once a head coach should be a sounding board for the boss, not a second voice telling him what to do.
Players you have coached before are worth bringing along; you already know what they can carry.
Outside noise comes with the job; the work in the building is what you control.

signatures: thanks the owner, general manager, staff and players in turn when looking back
names the backup who stepped in when asked about an injury-hit unit
takes the blame for a unit's flaw in plain terms before explaining the fix
want: to build a takeaway defense in Chicago that makes him a coordinator teams covet again after his New Orleans firing
fear: that a thin pass rush and a step back in takeaways expose the 2025 defense as luck rather than design
voice: Even-keeled, reserved and businesslike, with a dry streak of humor. He answers carefully, takes responsibility in plain terms when the unit falls short, and shrugs off outside criticism as part of the job. He praises players' effort and singles out the ones who step up from the bench.

evidence.summary: Promoted to replace Payton, his longtime boss, he says his main lesson from 8-28 in Oakland is to do things his own way, feels better prepared, will keep much of the structure, and declines early comment on a player's arrest until he has information. Loomis praises his leadership and teaching.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (Saints News Network), Ross Jackson
evidence.summary: Cornerback Alontae Taylor says he enjoys playing for Allen, recalls Allen asking for more swagger and energy in practice, and values being allowed to be himself while still playing physical defense. One player's view.

Entering year three, Mathieu says he seems more self-assured and outspoken, Jordan senses urgency, and Allen dismisses outside scrutiny as part of coaching. He replaced Payton's offensive coordinator with Klint Kubiak and chose most of his staff. Beat piece with player quotes.

His statement after the firing thanks Benson and Loomis, admits the team fell short, praises his staff, tells players he never doubted their commitment, and thanks fans. Gracious and reflective; a prepared statement.

First Chicago press conference: he wants an attacking, physical defense that takes the fight to offenses, has not settled how often to blitz, and sees pieces across the roster. Johnson reached out late in 2024 about joining him; Allen praises Johnson's creativity, work ethic and vision and says he will be a sounding board, not someone who tells the head coach what to do. Upbeat and humble. Team site.

His defense leads the league with 30 takeaways and 21 interceptions. He leaned on players he coached before (Nahshon Wright, C.J. Gardner-Johnson, D'Marco Jackson) when injuries hit, added more man coverage and blitzes, and likens game planning to cooking with whatever ingredients are on hand. Jaylon Johnson calls him aggressive; he and Ben Johnson talk daily and trust grew over time.

Offseason media session: he says the review of 2025 pointed at him, that installing a big new scheme crowded out fundamentals and technique, and that 2026 coaching will shift toward execution. Cites the line's poor 2025 pass-rush and run-stop win rates. Aggregated quotes; page shows only an update date.
